items.prompt: Define the product offering. [2]
items.canonical_answer: A product is the good or service offered to meet a customer need. It includes relevant features, quality, design and supporting service rather than only a physical object. A repair service is a product offering even though the customer is not simply buying a newly manufactured item. Product is distinct from production, the process of creating the offering. Customers judge whether benefits meet their purpose at an acceptable price. A technically impressive feature may add cost without value if buyers do not need it.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A product is the good or service offered to meet a customer need.

items.prompt: Distinguish between a consumer durable and a producer good using the two freezer purchases. A fictional household buys a freezer for its food; a fictional meal business buys a freezer to support production. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Consumer products are bought for personal or household use; producer or capital goods are used by businesses to produce other goods or services. Durable goods are used repeatedly over time, while non-durable goods are used up more quickly. Services provide an activity or benefit rather than ownership of a new physical good. Classify using purpose and characteristics: the same item can be a household consumer durable or business equipment depending on who buys it and why. The categories can overlap because they answer different questions. The first is a consumer durable, the second business equipment or a capital good. Both are physical durable items; buying purpose changes the consumer/producer distinction.
marking_guidance: Difference: Consumer products are bought for personal or household use; producer or capital goods are used by businesses to produce other goods or services.

items.prompt: Define product life cycle. [2]
items.canonical_answer: A product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from introduction, through growth and maturity, and finally decline. It is a model of sales through time, not a promise of identical timing for every product. Introduction commonly involves low initial sales and awareness-building; growth brings rising sales; maturity involves slower growth or a plateau; decline involves falling sales. Development can precede introduction, but sales have not yet begun. Managers can use evidence to consider changes, while recognising a temporary fall does not prove permanent decline.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A product life cycle describes the stages a product passes through from introduction, through growth and maturity, and finally decline.

items.prompt: Draw a labelled product-life-cycle model with sales and time axes and explain its stages. Construct an illustrative life cycle for a fictional lunch-container range, with no numerical sales data provided. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
Put time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis. Draw low introductory sales, a rising growth section, a high flatter maturity section and a declining section. Label the stages so the reader can distinguish the changes in the sales pattern. Some descriptions distinguish saturation within the mature plateau. The curve is conceptual unless data are supplied; do not present it as actual measured sales or assume a given number of years per stage. Extension actions such as adapting the product or finding new buyers can sometimes prolong sales but do not guarantee revival. ![Product life cycle](diagrams/product-life-cycle.png)

The labelled diagram shows the model’s changing sales direction rather than forecasts for a real range. Maturity does not mean zero sales, and decline is falling sales rather than necessarily an immediate end to all demand.
marking_guidance: Input: Put time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis.

items.prompt: State two features that can support a successful product. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Useful success features include meeting a real need, reliable quality, suitable design, value at the price, accessible supply and appropriate differentiation. items.prompt: Distinguish between the name, image and loyalty in Oru’s bag example. Fictional Oru Gear names its bag “Tana”. Buyers associate it with durability and some repeatedly choose it. [6]
items.canonical_answer: A brand name identifies an offering and distinguishes it from competitors. Brand loyalty is repeated preference and purchasing of that brand. Brand image is the identity or impression associated with it. A business can choose a name and communicate an intended image, but customers’ actual experiences influence the image they hold. Recognition is not itself loyalty: someone may know the name and still buy a rival. A strong image can support differentiation, but it needs credible quality and service rather than unsupported claims. Tana is the name; the durability association is image; repeated choice is loyalty. They are connected but not definitions of the same thing.
marking_guidance: Difference: A brand name identifies an offering and distinguishes it from competitors.

items.prompt: Define brand loyalty. [2]

items.canonical_answer: Packaging is the physical container or wrapping for a product, also used for promotional purposes. items.prompt: Define price. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Price is the monetary value that you pay for something or that something costs. For the customer it is part of the sacrifice made to obtain the offering; for the seller it affects revenue and the surplus after costs. Price interacts with perceived quality, competition, affordability and demand. A higher price can increase revenue per unit while reducing quantity sold; a lower price can increase volume without necessarily increasing profit. Distinguish the price paid by the customer from the producer’s cost of making the item.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Price is the monetary value that you pay for something or that something costs.

items.prompt: Explain why a low initial entry price and a high skimming price suit different conditions. Fictional Teya Drink enters a competitive local market with a familiar product, while fictional Omi Devices introduces a distinctive design valued by a small early market. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Cost-plus pricing adds a mark-up to a relevant unit-cost base. Penetration sets a low initial price to encourage market entry and customer trial. Skimming sets a high initial price for a distinctive new offering where some buyers will pay, often reducing it later. Competitive pricing uses rivals’ prices as a reference. Promotional pricing makes a temporary price reduction or special offer. Choose according to objectives, demand, competition, costs, product and capacity. A strategy is a pricing approach, not proof of customer response. A low price cannot compensate for an unwanted or unavailable product. Penetration may help Teya attract trial if it can afford the low price; skimming may suit Omi only if the distinctive benefit supports willingness to pay and rivals cannot immediately remove it.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Cost-plus pricing adds a mark-up to a relevant unit-cost base.

items.prompt: Define promotion in marketing. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Promotion is the entire set of activities which communicate the product, brand, service or business to customers. It can inform, persuade, remind or support relationships. items.prompt: Distinguish between radio, image-based local notices and an online buying route for Ota’s product. Fictional Ota Crafts wants local buyers to see the shape of a product. Some buyers access local online notices; others rely on a shop display. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Media include print, radio, television, outdoor displays and online channels. Compare audience reach, cost, targeting, message detail, access and the need for sound or images. Radio can reach listeners without showing a detailed design; print or online images can show it but require suitable access and attention.
